claims.claim: Bumetanide, a sulfamoyl anthranilic acid loop diuretic sharing the query's acid-sulfamoyl core, has an absolute oral bioavailability of 95% in cirrhosis patients after oral versus IV dosing (n=8), with L2 context reporting 95-100%.
Cirrhosis-condition contexts for metoclopramide and tolfenamic acid show high oral bioavailability (79-82% and about 100%, respectively), supporting a pattern of high F in cirrhosis.

Azosemide, the closest structural analog (tetrazole/thiophene bioisostere of the query), has an L1 absolute oral bioavailability of 20.4% in fasted healthy humans, meeting the F>=20% threshold; the L2 urinary-recovery estimate of 10% is indirect and does not overturn the L1 value.

L5 gut-wall efflux/intestinal-metabolism records concern 5-ASA, sulfasalazine, AVN 2f, labetalol, and salicylic acid; C60 uses furosemide only as a 1 mM modulator in a sulfasalazine Caco-2 experiment and does not measure furosemide's own permeability or bioavailability; C57/C63/C66 are duplicate representations of the same sulfasalazine/Ko143 experiment. None provide query-specific presystemic-loss evidence.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability measurement for furosemide itself is supplied.
No gut-wall efflux or intestinal-metabolism record for furosemide, bumetanide, or azosemide is supplied; L5 records are for unrelated molecules, with C60 using furosemide only as a modulator.
Azosemide was studied in fasted healthy subjects, not cirrhosis, and has conflicting estimates (20.4% L1 absolute vs 10% L2 urinary recovery).
Cirrhosis effects on furosemide-specific transporters and first-pass metabolism are not directly measured.
Furosemide's furan, chloro, and carboxylate groups may alter transporter/metabolic handling relative to bumetanide and azosemide.

The indirect azosemide urinary-recovery estimate of 10% and the physicochemical low-permeability prior are insufficient to support F<20%.
